topic: running a small smokehouse for hams and curing bitter, patchy smoke

provenance.author: glowny-en-a
provenance.notes: 10 turns, user first; variant a is cure-sheet arithmetic on the same hams with closed task questions, base is a diagnosis of bitter, patchy smoke. Grounded external referent: the smoker, introduced in turn 0 and central to the whole diagnosis (its damp dust, weak draw and tarred stack are the suspects, and every fix runs through it).

a: Here are five hams for the cure sheet, and their weights need listing from heaviest down.
The first ham weighs eleven kilograms and the second ham weighs nine kilograms exactly.
The third weighs eight kilograms, and the fourth weighs seven kilograms on the same scale.
The fifth ham is the lightest of the group at six kilograms even on the dial.
How many kilograms do the five hams come to when all the weights are added?
base: Our last three rounds of hams have come out bitter at the surface and patchy in colour.
We cure them three weeks in the larder, then hang them over beech dust to take smoke.
The smoker is a brick box in the yard with a firebox below and a tall stack.
The bitterness sits only in the outer finger of meat, and the middle still tastes clean.
What would you check first before we hang the next dozen hams in there?

a: Listed heaviest down, the order runs first, then second, then third, then fourth, then fifth.
The running totals after each ham are eleven, then twenty, then twenty-eight kilograms so far.
The last two totals are thirty-five and then forty-one kilograms across the whole group.
Cure salt at forty grams for each kilogram gives the first ham four hundred forty grams.
Does the group total of forty-one kilograms match the figure on the delivery note?
base: Bitter surface with patchy colour nearly always means the fire is smouldering too cool and wet.
Damp dust throws heavy tar, and tar is what lands on the rind as bitterness.
Check where the beech dust is stored, because a shed floor can wet it from below.
Then watch how the smoker draws on a still morning with the firebox door half open.
Does the smoke leave the stack in a thin blue line or roll out grey and thick?

a: Now work out the cure salt for the other four hams at the same forty grams.
List the salt for all five hams in the heaviest to lightest order used above.
Sugar goes in at ten grams for each kilogram, rounded to the nearest five grams.
Put the two heaviest hams on hook row one and the other three on row two.
Which salt weight belongs to the third ham at that fixed rate of forty grams?
base: The smoke rolls out grey and thick, and it hangs around the yard on quiet days.
The smoker draws well enough in wind, but on still mornings it barely pulls at all.
Our beech dust sits in an open barrel by the door, and the bottom half feels damp.
The brine tub shares the same shed, so splash and steam reach the barrel every week.
Would drier dust alone bring back the clean colour we had in the spring rounds?

a: The second ham takes three hundred sixty grams of salt at the stated rate.
The third takes three hundred twenty grams, and the fourth takes two hundred eighty grams.
The fifth ham takes two hundred forty grams of salt to finish the list.
Row one therefore carries salt of eight hundred grams across its two heavy hams together.
Row two carries eight hundred forty grams, and its sugar comes to two hundred ten grams.
base: Drier dust will thin the smoke, but the weak draw on still mornings needs fixing too.
Move the dust barrel out of that shed and keep only a dry week's worth indoors.
A stack that only pulls in wind is usually too short or choked with old tar.
Sweep the stack, then burn a hot bare flame for an hour to dry the flue.
After that the smoker should pull steadily even when the yard air is not moving.

a: One correction before we go on: the fourth ham weighs seven and a half kilograms.
Recalculate its salt and its sugar, and leave the other four hams exactly as listed.
Then give the new totals for weight and for salt across the whole group of five.
After that, list the hams in the order they enter the box next week.
Which ham goes in first under the order second, then fourth, then first, then third?
base: We swept the stack and a bucket of black flakes came down from the first metre.
The bare flame burned for an hour and the draw improved before the fire was out.
This morning the smoker pulled a thin blue line of smoke on a dead calm day.
The dust barrel now lives in the feed room, which stays dry through the winter.
Should the next dozen hams hang higher in the box than the last lot did?

a: At seven and a half kilograms the fourth ham takes three hundred grams of salt.
Its sugar becomes seventy-five grams, and the group weight rises to forty-one and a half.
The new salt total across five hams is one thousand six hundred sixty grams.
The entry order stands as second, then fourth, then first, then third, then fifth last.
The second ham therefore enters first, and the fifth ham closes the loading next week.
base: Hang them a hand's width higher, because the lowest hooks catch the fiercest swings of heat.
Blue smoke and a steady draw mean the box will hold a gentle even warmth now.
Give the first pair eight hours, then rest them a day before you judge the colour.
Salt balance matters as well, so weigh the cure at forty grams for each kilogram.
Keep a written page for every round, with dust, hours and weather noted beside the date.

a: Convert the hanging plan into rounds that take twelve hams in the box each time.
Tell me how many full rounds cover thirty-two hams and how many hooks stay empty.
Then split the salt total into two even tubs and give the figure for each.
The first round starts on Monday, with the following rounds ten days apart on the sheet.
How many full rounds does thirty-two hams come to at twelve for every round?
base: The first pair came out an even chestnut brown with no bitterness at the rind.
Their weight loss was nine percent, which the old books say is right for this style.
Our neighbour wants twenty hams for his shop before Easter on top of our own orders.
The box holds twelve hams at a time when they hang with space to breathe.
Can two rounds a fortnight apart cover thirty-two hams before the Easter week arrives?

a: Thirty-two hams make two full rounds with eight hams left for a third shorter round.
The third round therefore runs with four empty hooks out of its twelve places.
Each of the two tubs holds eight hundred thirty grams of salt when the total splits evenly.
Round one starts Monday the first, and round two starts Thursday the eleventh.
Round three starts Sunday the twenty-first, keeping the ten day spacing all the way through.
base: Two rounds of twelve give twenty-four, so you would land eight hams short of the need.
Three rounds cover it with four hooks spare, if the curing dates are staggered early.
Start the first cure now, the second ten days later, and the third ten days after that.
Each round then meets the box just as the one before it comes out to rest.
The last hams finish a clear week before Easter, leaving time for resting and wrapping.

a: Write out a four step round sheet for the crew in the order set down here.
Step one is salting, step two is resting, step three is rinsing the legs.
Step four is hanging, and every step needs its own dates marked on the sheet.
Salting runs twenty-one days and resting runs seven days for every leg on the list.
Rinsing takes one day, and hanging in the box takes eight hours for each round.
base: We salted the first sixteen legs yesterday and the second batch goes into cure on Friday.
My daughter keeps the written pages now, one line for every ham with its dates.
The feed room shelf holds three dry sacks of beech dust, enough for all three rounds.
We will sweep the stack again between rounds and burn the drying flame each time.
If the weather turns wet, the spare tarpaulin goes over the woodpile the same day.

a: Step one for round one runs from Monday the first to Monday the twenty-second.
Step two then runs seven days, ending on Monday the twenty-ninth for that round.
Step three falls on Tuesday the thirtieth, with the legs rinsed and wiped by evening.
Step four fills the following day, with all twelve legs hanging their eight hours together.
The sheet repeats for rounds two and three with every date shifted ten days along.
base: That plan holds together, and the staggered cures are the part most people get wrong.
Check the deepest part of each leg with a skewer when it leaves the cure.
A clean smell at the bone means the salt has done its work all the way through.
Weigh two marked hams from every round and note the loss beside their dates.
By Easter the pages will show a method you can repeat every winter without guessing.
